name: Commercial Poultry Production
objectives: Given your market, money and time, choose broilers, layers or improved indigenous chickens and give reasons, naming at least three reasons that fit your farm and buyers

Before the chicks arrive and during brooding, prepare the house, set the number of birds for the space, and adjust brooder heat by watching the chicks, with the house ready a day ahead and chicks spread evenly under the heat

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Broilers, layers or improved indigenous chickens
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose the type of chicken that fits your market, money and time.
This lesson builds toward: Given your market, money and time, you will choose broilers, layers or improved indigenous chickens and give reasons, naming at least three reasons that fit your farm and buyers.
Broilers are bred for meat. They grow very fast and are often sold within about 5 to 7 weeks, depending on the breed and the weight buyers want. Money comes back quickly, but they need high-quality feed, close care and a ready buyer on the day they are ready: every extra day eats feed and profit.
Layers are bred for eggs. They start laying at about 4 to 5 months and lay for more than a year, so you feed them for months before any income, and you need a steady egg market. Improved indigenous or dual-purpose chickens sit in between: they are hardier than broilers and layers, can scavenge with some extra feed, and sell for meat and eggs, often at a better price per bird, but grow and lay less than commercial hybrids.
Examples: Kenbro, sold by Kenchic in Kenya, is a dual-purpose bird; Kenchic says it is ready for meat at about 10 to 14 weeks or lays from about 25 weeks, but will not reach the production of specialised broilers or layers. The Kuroiler, developed in India, is a dual-purpose scavenging bird; a study in Uganda found Kuroilers grew heavier than local chickens under village conditions. Buy any breed only from a hatchery your livestock office or vet trusts, and ask other farmers how it performed for them.
Step by step:
- Write who will buy: live birds, meat, eggs, hotels, markets.
- Write how much money you can spend before income starts.
- Write how much time you can give each day.
- Compare broilers, layers and improved indigenous birds against your lists.
- Choose one, with three reasons, and a trusted hatchery.
Words to know:
- Broiler: a chicken bred to grow fast for meat.
- Layer: a chicken bred to lay many eggs.
- Improved indigenous chicken: a hardier dual-purpose bird bred from or for local conditions, kept for meat and eggs.
- Hatchery: a business that hatches and sells day-old chicks.
Official sources:
- Kenchic: Kenbro (dual-purpose improved indigenous chicken)
- Sharma et al. 2015, Livestock Research for Rural Development: Kuroiler vs indigenous chickens in Uganda
Try it now: Write your three lists: buyers, money available before income, and daily time. Choose broilers, layers or improved indigenous birds and write three reasons, plus the name of a hatchery your livestock office or vet trusts.
You can now choose broilers, layers or improved indigenous chickens to fit your market, money and time.

check.q: A farmer has little money to wait and a hotel that buys meat birds every six weeks. Which type fits best?
check.why: Broilers are sold within weeks, matching a regular meat buyer and a short wait for income.

check.q: What does Kenchic say about Kenbro compared with specialised broilers and layers?
options: It will not reach their production levels
It needs no feed at all
check.why: Kenbro is hardier and dual-purpose but does not match the output of specialised hybrids.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Housing, space and brooding chicks
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Prepare the house, set the number of birds for the space, and brood chicks at the right warmth.
This lesson builds toward: Before the chicks arrive and during brooding, you will prepare the house, set the number of birds for the space, and adjust brooder heat by watching the chicks, with the house ready a day ahead and chicks spread evenly under the heat.
A good poultry house is dry, airy and safe. In hot areas, open sides with strong wire mesh let air through; a long house is often set east to west so less sun shines in, with a roof overhang to keep rain out. Use deep, dry litter such as wood shavings or rice husks. Keep out rats, snakes, wild birds and thieves. Before chicks arrive, clean and disinfect the empty house and equipment and leave it empty for the rest period your vet advises.
Space: crowding causes heat stress, wet litter, pecking and disease. Your hatchery, breed guide or extension officer gives the number of birds per square metre for your breed, age and house. Multiply the floor area by that number. Example only: a 5 m by 8 m house is 40 square metres; if your guide says 10 broilers per square metre at market age, it holds 400 broilers, not 500.
Brooding: day-old chicks cannot keep themselves warm. Set up a brooder ring (a circle of card or metal sheet) with litter, a heat source (gas or electric brooder, bulbs, or a charcoal stove with good ventilation, because charcoal fumes can kill), feeders and drinkers, and heat it before the chicks arrive. University of Missouri Extension gives about 32 to 35 °C under the heater in the first week, then about 3 °C less each week. Watch the chicks: huddled under the heat means too cold; far away and panting means too hot; crowded on one side means a draught; spread evenly means just right.
Step by step:
- Clean and disinfect the empty house and equipment; rest it as the vet advises.
- Spread deep, dry litter.
- Work out how many birds the floor holds from your breed guide.
- Set up the brooder ring, heat source, feeders and drinkers.
- Heat it before the chicks arrive.
- Watch the chicks several times a day and adjust the heat.
Words to know:
- Brooding: keeping young chicks warm and fed in their first weeks.
- Brooder ring: a circle of card or metal sheet that keeps chicks near the heat, feed and water.
- Litter: dry bedding on the floor, such as wood shavings or rice husks.
- Stocking density: how many birds are kept per square metre of floor.
Official sources:
- University of Missouri Extension G8351: Brooding and growing chicks (temperature by week, chick behaviour)
- FAO: Good biosecurity practices in small scale commercial and scavenging poultry production systems in Kenya
Try it now: Measure your poultry house (or a planned one) and work out the floor area. Ask your hatchery or extension officer how many birds per square metre for your breed, and write how many birds it holds. Sketch your brooder set-up.
You can now prepare a house, set the number of birds for its space, and brood chicks by watching how they behave.

check.q: Your chicks are all huddled tightly under the heater. What does it mean?
options: They are ready to leave the brooder
They are too cold; add heat or block draughts
check.why: Huddling under the heat means the chicks are cold.

check.q: Your house is 6 m by 5 m. The guide says 10 birds per square metre. How many birds?

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Feeding and water by stage
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan the feed for each stage, when to change it, and a constant supply of clean water.
This lesson builds toward: For each stage of your batch, you will plan the feed type, the change dates and the water supply, with clean water available all the time and every stage covered.
Feed is the biggest cost of a batch, so feed the right feed at the right stage. Broilers: broiler starter, then broiler finisher (some programmes add a grower). Layers: chick mash, then growers mash, then layers mash from the point of lay, which has the extra calcium hens need for strong shells. Improved indigenous birds: follow the hatchery's guide; under semi-free-range they still need a balanced feed on top of scavenging to grow and lay well. Change feeds over a few days by mixing old and new.
Buy feed from a trusted miller, check the bag is labelled, dry and within date, and store it on pallets in a dry place. Use enough feeders so all birds can eat at once, raise them to the height of the birds' backs as they grow, and do not fill them to the brim, because birds scratch feed out and waste it.
Water matters more than feed: chickens drink more water than they eat feed, and they stop eating and laying when water runs out or gets hot. Give clean, cool water all the time, with enough drinkers, cleaned every day. A sudden drop in water use is often the first sign of sickness. If you give a vaccine or medicine in water, follow the vet and label exactly; some need water without chlorine or disinfectant.
Step by step:
- Write the stages for your type of bird.
- Write the feed for each stage and the age to change.
- Plan enough feeders and drinkers for all birds at once.
- Raise feeders and drinkers as the birds grow; do not overfill.
- Clean drinkers daily; never let water run out.
- Note daily water use; a sudden drop means call the vet.
Words to know:
- Starter: the first, high-protein feed for young chicks.
- Finisher: the last feed for broilers before sale.
- Layers mash: feed for laying hens with extra calcium for eggshells.
- Point of lay: the age when young hens are about to start laying.
Official sources:
- FAO: Good biosecurity practices in small scale commercial and scavenging poultry production systems in Kenya
Try it now: Make a feed table for your batch: stage, age, feed type, and roughly how many bags you expect to buy (ask your feed supplier or hatchery). Add how many feeders and drinkers you need and who cleans the drinkers each day.
You can now plan the right feed for each stage, when to change it, and a constant supply of clean water.

check.q: Why do laying hens need layers mash rather than growers mash?
options: It has the extra calcium needed for strong eggshells
check.why: Laying hens need extra calcium for shells, which layers mash supplies.

check.q: Your broilers suddenly drink much less water than yesterday. What does this suggest?
options: They may be getting sick; check them and call the vet
It is time to sell them
check.why: A sudden drop in water use is often the first sign of disease.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: A vaccination programme and batch biosecurity
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a vaccination programme with your vet and set biosecurity rules for the batch.
This lesson builds toward: With your vet or animal health officer, you will write a vaccination programme and batch biosecurity rules, and record each vaccination, with every vaccine date set by the vet and no vaccine given outside the programme.
Vaccination protects the batch from diseases that are common in your area. Which vaccines, at what age and how they are given (drinking water, eye drop, injection or wing stab) must be set by a registered vet or animal health officer, because diseases differ by area and season. Common examples in Africa include Newcastle disease and Gumboro, plus Marek's disease (often given at the hatchery) and fowl pox; your vet may add others. Ask the hatchery for a record of what the chicks already received.
Make the vaccines work: buy from a licensed agrovet, check the expiry date, keep them cool from the shop to the birds, give them exactly as the label and vet say, vaccinate the whole flock, and write the date, vaccine, batch number and method in your records. Never treat sick birds with antibiotics on your own: the vet decides, and you record the withdrawal period from the label so no eggs or meat are sold before it ends.
Batch biosecurity: buy chicks from one trusted hatchery and run the house all-in, all-out (all birds the same age, in together and out together). Between batches, remove all litter, wash and disinfect the house and equipment, and leave it empty for the rest period your vet advises. Keep visitors out, use a footbath and farm boots, keep wild birds and rats away, and never bring market birds home. Avian influenza is notifiable: sudden deaths, swollen purple combs, gasping or a sharp egg drop mean keep birds in, stop all sales and movement, and call the vet at once.
Step by step:
- Ask the hatchery what vaccines the chicks already received.
- Sit with your vet and write the programme: disease, age, method.
- Buy vaccines from a licensed agrovet; check expiry; keep them cool.
- Vaccinate the whole flock exactly as the label and vet say; record it.
- Run all-in, all-out; clean, disinfect and rest the house between batches.
- Suspected avian influenza or Newcastle disease: keep birds in, stop sales, call the vet.
Words to know:
- Vaccination programme: a written plan of which vaccines the flock gets, at what age and how, set by the vet.
- All-in, all-out: all birds in a house are the same age, placed together and removed together.
- Withdrawal period: the time after a medicine before eggs or meat can be sold; it is on the label.
- Licensed agrovet: a shop allowed by law to sell animal medicines and vaccines.
Official sources:
- World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH): Newcastle disease
- World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH): Avian influenza
- USDA APHIS: Avian influenza (signs in birds)
- FAO: Good biosecurity practices in small scale commercial and scavenging poultry production systems in Kenya
- FAO: Prudent and efficient use of antimicrobials in pigs and poultry (vets, health plans, withdrawal periods)
- Kenya Veterinary Board (register of vets and veterinary para-professionals)
- Veterinary Council of Nigeria (register of veterinary surgeons)
Try it now: Book a talk with your vet or animal health officer. Bring a table with columns: disease, age, method, date given, batch number. Fill in the programme the vet sets. Under it, write five biosecurity rules for your batch.
You can now write a vaccination programme with your vet, record each vaccination, and run strict batch biosecurity.

check.q: Who should decide which vaccines your flock gets and when?
options: A registered vet or animal health officer
check.why: Diseases differ by area, so a registered vet sets the programme.

options: Birds go out to scavenge every day
Visitors may come in and out freely
New birds are added every week
All birds in a house are placed and removed together
check.why: One age group per house lets you clean and rest it fully between batches, breaking disease cycles.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Egg handling and flock records
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Collect and store eggs correctly and keep daily flock records.
This lesson builds toward: Every day of the batch, you will collect and store eggs correctly and record birds, deaths, feed, eggs and treatments, with no missing days in the record.
Eggs lose quality and pick up germs if they sit in nests. Collect at least twice a day, more in hot weather. Keep nests clean with fresh litter so eggs come out clean. Separate cracked, dirty and very small eggs. Clean lightly soiled eggs with a dry cloth; do not soak them in water, which can pull germs through the shell. Store eggs in trays, pointed end down, in a cool, shaded, airy place away from strong smells, and sell the oldest first.
Records tell you what is happening before it is too late. Every day write: number of birds, deaths and their likely cause, feed used, water used, and eggs collected (by tray and grade). Also record each vaccination and treatment, the withdrawal end date from the label, every purchase and every sale. A paper book works; a phone spreadsheet adds the totals for you.
Use the records. Mortality rate = birds dead / birds started x 100. Laying rate = eggs collected in a day / hens x 100. If deaths rise, water use falls or the laying rate drops suddenly, check the flock and call the vet. At the end of the batch, the records give you the numbers for your cost sheet.
Step by step:
- Collect eggs at least twice a day.
- Separate cracked, dirty and small eggs; dry-clean lightly soiled ones.
- Store in trays, pointed end down, cool and shaded; oldest first.
- Each day record birds, deaths, feed, water and eggs.
- Record vaccinations, treatments, withdrawal end dates, purchases and sales.
- Work out mortality and laying rate each week and look for sudden changes.
Words to know:
- Mortality rate: the share of birds that died, as a percent of the birds you started with.
- Laying rate: eggs collected in a day as a percent of the number of hens.
- Grade: sorting eggs by size and quality.
Official sources:
- FAO: Good biosecurity practices in small scale commercial and scavenging poultry production systems in Kenya
Try it now: Make a daily record page with columns: date, birds, deaths and cause, feed used, water used, eggs collected, notes. Fill in an example week. Then work out the mortality rate and, for layers, the laying rate for one day.
You can now collect and store eggs correctly and keep daily records that show mortality and laying rate.

check.q: How should eggs be stored in trays?
options: Pointed end up, in the sun
Pointed end down, in a cool, shaded place
check.why: Pointed end down, cool and shaded keeps eggs fresh longer.

check.q: You started with 500 broilers and 25 died. What is the mortality rate?

lessons.title: Lesson 6: The economics of a batch: cost per bird and break-even
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate the cost per bird or per tray and the break-even price for a batch.
This lesson builds toward: Using your local prices and expected mortality, you will calculate the cost per bird sold or per tray and the break-even price for a batch, with every cost included and correct arithmetic.
List every cost of the batch: chicks, feed, vaccines and vet, litter, brooding fuel or electricity, disinfectant, labour, transport and packaging. Example with made-up Kenya shilling prices, 500 broilers: chicks 50,000; feed 122,500; vaccines and vet 5,000; litter, brooding and power 8,000; transport and other 6,500. Total KES 192,000. Use your own quotes: prices differ by place and season, and in NGN, GHS or XOF the method is the same.
Mortality changes everything, because dead birds still ate feed. If 5 percent die, you sell 475 birds. Cost per bird sold = 192,000 / 475 = KES 404. That is your break-even price: sell below it and you lose money. If 15 percent die, you sell only 425, and the break-even rises to about KES 452. At a selling price of KES 550, 475 birds bring 261,250, a profit of 69,250. To find how many birds you must sell to cover costs: 192,000 / 550 = 349.1, so 350 birds.
Layers: work weekly. Example: 300 hens at an 80 percent laying rate give 300 x 0.8 x 7 = 1,680 eggs, or 56 trays of 30. If feed and other costs are KES 15,000 a week, the cost per tray is 15,000 / 56 = about KES 268. Compare it with the price buyers pay. Before you start, also read any loan or contract with a buyer or supplier fully, and ask a trusted adviser.
Step by step:
- List every cost of the batch with your local prices.
- Add them up for the total cost.
- Estimate mortality and work out birds you will sell.
- Cost per bird = total cost / birds sold: your break-even price.
- Layers: cost per tray = weekly costs / trays collected.
- Compare with the selling price; work out profit or loss.
Words to know:
- Break-even price: the price per bird or tray at which income just covers all costs.
- Profit: income minus all costs.
- Cost sheet: a list of every cost of the batch with the totals.
Try it now: Final task: write your costed plan for one batch: type of bird, house size and number of birds, brooding set-up, feeds by stage, vaccination programme and biosecurity rules, records, and a cost sheet with every cost, expected mortality, cost per bird sold or per tray, and your break-even price.
You can now cost a batch, allow for mortality, and work out your cost per bird or per tray and your break-even price.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Type of bird and market No reason for the choice, or no buyer named. Names the type of bird, a trusted hatchery and at least three reasons that fit the market, money and time. Names a specific buyer and when they buy, and plans the batch to match. House, space and brooding Number of birds not worked out from the floor area, or no brooding plan. Floor area x birds per square metre from the guide; brooder set-up with heat checked by chick behaviour. Also covers cleaning, disinfecting and resting the house and safe ventilation for the heat source. Feed and water plan Stages or feed types missing, or no water plan. Feed type for each stage, change dates, enough feeders and drinkers, and clean water all the time. Estimates bags of feed per stage and who checks water daily. Vaccination and biosecurity No vet involved, or doses invented, or no biosecurity rules. Programme set by a registered vet, recorded; all-in, all-out and at least four biosecurity rules; avian influenza reporting. Includes the vet's name and number and the hatchery's vaccination record. Records No daily record plan. Daily record of birds, deaths, feed, water and eggs, plus vaccinations, treatments and sales. Shows how mortality and laying rate will be checked each week. Cost sheet and break-even Costs missing, mortality ignored, or arithmetic wrong. Every cost listed, mortality allowed for, correct cost per bird or tray and break-even price. Compares break-even with real buyer prices and shows profit at two mortality levels. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the plan and check it again.

check.q: A batch costs NGN 900,000 and you expect to sell 450 birds. What is the break-even price per bird?
Why does higher mortality raise your cost per bird?
options: Dead birds ate feed and cost money but are not sold
Dead birds are sold at a higher price
check.why: The same total cost is shared by fewer birds sold.
